patterns.name: Spring controller registered without method-level security annotation
patterns.description: A Spring MVC or Spring Boot controller file does not apply any method-level or class-level security annotation. Spring Security's primary per-endpoint auth mechanisms are @PreAuthorize (SpEL expression, e.g. hasRole('ADMIN')), @Secured (role names), and @RolesAllowed (JSR-250). Without these, endpoints are accessible to any authenticated — or even unauthenticated — user depending on your SecurityFilterChain configuration. This check fires on controller files (matching *Controller.java, */controller/*.java, etc.) that import Spring Web annotations but call no recognised security annotation. NOTE: if your project uses a global SecurityFilterChain that restricts all endpoints via .anyRequest().authenticated(), this is an informational finding. Use @PermitAll on intentionally public endpoints to suppress.
patterns.message: Spring controller file {file} does not call any security annotation (@PreAuthorize, @Secured, @RolesAllowed). All endpoints in this file may be accessible without proper authorization checks. Apply @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ROLE')") to each handler method, or add a class-level @Secured annotation. If global auth is enforced via SecurityFilterChain, add @PermitAll to intentionally public endpoints.

patterns.name: Jakarta EE JAX-RS resource without authorization annotation
patterns.description: A Jakarta EE (JAX-RS) resource class does not apply any authorization annotation. JAX-RS security is declared via JSR-250 annotations: @RolesAllowed specifies which roles may call the endpoint, @PermitAll explicitly grants all users access (including unauthenticated), and @DenyAll explicitly blocks all access. Without any annotation, endpoint access is governed by the container's default security policy — which is typically to allow all authenticated users, or in some containers, unauthenticated access. This check fires on JAX-RS resource files (importing jakarta.ws.rs or javax.ws.rs) that lack any recognized authorization annotation. Note: this check covers both jakarta.ws.rs (Jakarta EE 9+) and javax.ws.rs (Jakarta EE 8 / Java EE) namespaces.
patterns.message: Jakarta EE JAX-RS resource file {file} does not declare any authorization annotation (@RolesAllowed, @PermitAll, or @DenyAll). Without explicit authorization, endpoint access depends on container defaults. Apply @RolesAllowed({"role"}) to restrict access, or @PermitAll for intentionally public endpoints.

patterns.name: Spring controller directly accesses repository (bypasses service layer)
patterns.description: A Spring controller class directly imports and uses a repository (JPA repository, Spring Data repository, or DAO) instead of delegating to a service layer. The standard Spring layered architecture is: Controller → Service → Repository → Database. Controllers are responsible for HTTP translation; business logic and data access belong in the service and repository layers respectively. Direct controller-to-repository access couples the HTTP layer to the data layer, makes the controller harder to unit test (requires a database or mock repository), and bypasses any transaction management or business rules in the service layer. This check fires when a controller file imports a class whose name ends in Repository or resides in a repository or dao package. Note: some simple CRUD microservices intentionally skip the service layer — treat this as a prompt to review, not a definitive violation.
patterns.message: Spring controller file {file} directly imports repository or data-access class '{target}'. Controllers should delegate data access to a service layer: Controller → Service → Repository → Database. Inject a @Service instead of the repository directly.
